description: Security enthusiasts by day, exploring nasa space challenge by night.
summary:
SpaceSweepers helps people make sense of NASA's microgravity combustion research. We pulled all 26 combustion investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, with their test tables, reports and DOIs, and turned 1,411 experimental tests into four ways to explore them: a Mission Fit ranking for a chosen habitat, an Envelope chart of every oxygen and pressure condition NASA has actually tested, the Flame Sweeper, which maps where flames burned or went out, and an SI Insights chat that searches 8,077 pieces of PSI evidence in plain language.

The challenge asks for SI-powered insights from messy data, so we built it to be trusted. SI proposes, code decides. A small open-source model (IBM Granite, running locally) writes short, cited answers, and a checker called Nimbus removes any claim, number or quote the PSI evidence doesn't support, and shows what it removed. Missing data is labelled unknown, never guessed.

This matters because fire safety in space depends on knowing what has really been tested, and where it hasn't. SpaceSweepers shows those gaps honestly, so researchers can trace every answer back to its source.
details:
What it is:

SpaceSweepers is a web dashboard for NASA's microgravity combustion research. The research is spread over 26 PSI investigations, in tables, reports and papers, and a language model asked about it can make numbers up. We built SpaceSweepers so every answer points back to its source, and so it says clearly what NASA has not tested.

How it works:

We pull all 26 PSI combustion investigations, with their test tables, reports and DOIs. 1,411 tests from 6 of those investigations were clean enough to compare. The app has seven views: Overview, Fire Safety, Rank (which investigations fit a Moon base, the ISS or a spacesuit), Correlation, Flame Sweeper (where flames burned or went out), SI Insights (a chat over 8,077 pieces of PSI evidence) and PSI Source (where the data comes from and how much of it we could use).

A small local model writes short, cited answers. A checker we call Nimbus then removes any claim, number or quote the evidence doesn't back up. Code does all the counting and ranking.

Who it's for and what it does for them:

It's for professors, graduate and undergraduate students, aerospace researchers and aerospace engineers.

SI Insights has a Guided and Expert switch, so each user gets the version that fits them:

  • Guided mode is for undergraduate students and anyone new to combustion research. It is a plain chat with starter questions, follow-ups that remember the last question, and the quotes, tests and sources beside each answer. Professors can use it to introduce the data in class.
  • Expert mode is for aerospace researchers, engineers and graduate students. It shows what Nimbus checked and removed and why, the tables with file and row, and a scenario form where you enter your own oxygen and pressure.

We hope it makes decades of NASA combustion research easier to find, compare and understand.

What's different about it:

We never let the model produce a number. When the data isn't there, we show a gap. Rank shows a range ("up to") for what it can't compute, and the Flame Sweeper leaves untested regions blank. Nimbus exists so the model can't invent outcomes.

What we thought about:

Unknown values are never shown as zero. The habitat atmospheres, weights and bands are our assumptions, and the pages say so. Different kinds of evidence are never added together. We used an open-source model and cite every investigation by DOI. We also state the limits: only 6 of 26 investigations have charted tests, PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data, and we refresh the data by hand.

How we used SI:

Two ways. Inside the product, IBM Granite 3.3 2B (open source, Apache-2.0) runs locally through Ollama. It writes short answers and points at evidence, and rules in our code check every sentence. Code computes the counts, rankings and tables. To build it, we used Claude Code (Anthropic) to help write and test the code and documentation. We decided the design, picked the data and the rules, and checked the results against 295 automated tests and our own evaluation questions.

How we used Agents(Nimbus):

Nimbus is how SpaceSweepers uses SI safely. A small local model reads messy text well and does arithmetic badly, so we split the work into seven small agents. Each has one narrow job, a fixed answer format and checking rules in code. The SI proposes and code decides. An agent never produces a number.

Preparing the data (run when the data is refreshed):

  • Investigator: labels each investigation experimental, simulation or both.
  • Table mapper: matches PSI table columns to our variables.
  • Pillar pointer: finds the sentence linking research to prevention, detection or suppression powers Fire-Safety view.
  • Outcome pointer: finds the lab note saying whether a sample burned.

Answering questions (run on demand):

  • Investigator: chooses which PSI lookups to run.
  • Analyst: writes the short, cited chat answer.
  • Definition pointer: finds PSI's own definition of a term.
  • Micro-Flame: explains the Flame Sweeper's patterns. This can be expanded based on NASA's internal calculation/methods for analyzing the data.

Each time, code gathers the evidence, an agent points or writes, code checks it, and the answer shows its sources. People can confirm a mapping by hand. In our own 16-question test, Nimbus removed 10 of the 37 sentences the model wrote.

NASA data:

PSI: 26 combustion investigations, each cited by DOI. The habitat atmospheres come from the Space Apps "Flame in Freefall" challenge page and are labelled as not PSI data.

Safety and Security Controls:

  • Browser protections: a strict content security policy with no inline scripts, text from data shown as plain text, host checks, rate limits and input validation.
  • Privacy: while building the dataset we found login credentials in a 2012 PSI file and stripped them. The pipeline now removes emails, phone numbers and username/password pairs by pattern before saving anything. The rule is in document.psy and replaces a pair with [credential removed]. We never download raw data, and the model only sees evidence our code selects.
  • SI safeguards, following the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications: the model proposes and code decides, and Nimbus removes any claim, number, link or instruction the evidence doesn't support.
  • Automated scans on every deploy: code (Semgrep, Bandit), dependencies (pip-audit, OSV-Scanner), secrets (Gitleaks, TruffleHog) and the container image (Grype).
  • Supply chain: pinned dependencies and GitHub Actions, a non-root container, and a signed image published with an SBOM and build provenance.
  • Findings: we fixed every scan finding except one Python finding that has no fixed image yet. It's documented, with a note on when to remove it.

Tools and hardware:

Python 3.14, FastAPI, SQLite, plain JavaScript and SVG, pytest, IBM Granite 3.3 2B through Ollama, Docker, GitHub and GitHub Actions, Claude Code, and Canva for the slides.
